content: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy (GSE), commonly known as celiac disease, is associated with a wide range of conditions, though its primary symptoms are typically confined to the gastrointestinal tract and related tissues. These include irritable bowel disease, eosinophilic gastroenteritis, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia. While these symptoms are well-documented in celiac disease, this discussion focuses on autoimmune and allergic-like responses (mediated by IgE, IgA, or IgG antibodies) that are significantly elevated in GSE. Many of these responses persist even on a strict gluten-free (GF) diet, becoming independent of celiac disease after being triggered. Clinical ambiguities arise because subclinical celiac disease can still promote secondary allergic and autoimmune diseases, even when undetected. Although the prevalence of autoimmune diseases in GSE patients is higher than in the general population, the association with secondary diseases remains largely idiopathic and sporadic, with low co-occurrence frequencies making statistical linkage difficult. Blood Disorders in GSE Vitamin Deficiencies: Malabsorption in GSE can lead to deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), vitamin B, and essential fatty acids, causing secondary complications. Hypocalcemia is also common. Even after treatment, prolonged intestinal damage and dietary restrictions may result in post-treatment deficiencies. Vitamin A: Poor absorption of vitamin A has been observed in celiac disease and may contribute to esophageal cancers associated with GSE. Folic Acid Deficiency: This deficiency is linked to megaloblastic anemia, brain calcifications, epilepsy, dementia, and visual disturbances. Vitamin B6 Deficiency: This can cause neuropathies and heightened pain sensitivity, potentially explaining peripheral neuropathies, pain, and depression in GSE. Vitamin B12 Deficiency: Associated with megaloblastic anemia and pernicious anemia. Vitamin D Deficiency: Leads to osteopenia, osteoporosis, and hypocalcemia. Vitamin K Deficiency: Identified in patients with bleeding disorders, treatable with vitamin K supplementation. Vitamin E Deficiency: Can result in central nervous system (CNS) issues and myopathy. Mineral Deficiencies: GSE is linked to deficiencies in calcium (causing osteopenia), magnesium (leading to parathyroid abnormalities), and selenium (potentially exacerbating autoimmune hyperthyroidism like Graves' disease). Blood Factors: Carnitine deficiency, childhood prolactin deficiency, and elevated homocysteine levels are associated with GSE. Anemia: Megaloblastic Anemia (MA): Caused by folate and B12 deficiencies, but unlike other forms, GSE-associated MA is not linked to autoimmune gastritis. Pernicious Anemia (PA): Results from malabsorption phenomena in GSE. Iron-Deficiency Anemia (IDA): Often the sole symptom of subclinical celiac disease, accompanied by low serum ferritin levels. While IDA typically resolves on a GF diet, refractory disease or gluten-sensitive malignancies can cause persistent IDA. Clotting Abnormalities Thromboembolism is a recognized complication of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with a threefold increased risk. Factor V Leiden mutation further elevates the risk of venous thrombosis. Studies have shown a co-occurrence between celiac disease and venous thrombosis. Dermatological Conditions Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH): Caused by triticeae glutens, with epidermal transglutaminase (eTG) as the autoantigen. All DH patients are either susceptible to or have celiac disease. DH is relatively rare, affecting about 5% of celiac patients. Other Skin Conditions: Aphthous stomatitis, chronic urticaria, eczema, and atopy disorders are more common in celiac patients and their first-degree relatives. Psoriasis and rare conditions like prurigo nodularis and Rothmund-Thomson syndrome have also been linked to GSE. Alopecia Areata: Associated with GSE, though hair regrowth does not always occur on a GF diet. Endocrine Disorders Autoimmune Thyroiditis: Graves' disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis are significantly more common in celiac patients. Selenium and other mineral deficiencies may contribute to this increased prevalence. Type 1 Diabetes (T1D): Juvenile-onset T1D is strongly associated with GSE, with evidence suggesting that GSE often precedes T1D. Gluten-free diets have shown some improvements in early juvenile diabetes patients. Anti-transglutaminase antibodies and gluten-specific T-cells are frequently elevated in T1D patients with GSE. Addison's Disease: Individuals with celiac disease are 11 times more likely to develop Addison's disease. Fertility Issues GSE can lead to infertility and high-risk pregnancies. Some infertile women with GSE also have iron deficiency anemia or zinc deficiency. Birth defects may be linked to folic acid deficiencies. GSE has also been identified as a rare cause of amenorrhea. Gastrointestinal Diseases Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): Diarrhea-dominant IBS is common in GSE, with increased serum IgG levels in treated and untreated celiac patients. Persistent IBS symptoms may result from undetected food intolerances, gut sensitivity, or yeast/bacterial overgrowth. Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD): Includes Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and microscopic colitis. IBD prevalence is increased tenfold in celiac disease. Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD): GERD in GSE may result from inflammation and delayed gastric emptying. While acid blockers can treat GERD, they may worsen preexisting hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Common in children with celiac disease, with improvement seen on GF or allergen-free diets. Neurological Disorders Peripheral Neuropathies: Common in GSE, potentially due to vitamin deficiencies and malabsorption of essential fatty acids. Guillain-Barré syndrome and anti-ganglioside autoantibodies are also associated with GSE. Ataxia: Gluten-sensitive ataxia is linked to GSE, with some patients showing antibodies reactive to Purkinje fibers. However, a large Swedish study found no association between GSE and ataxia. Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD): Some cases of ASD may be linked to GSE, possibly due to malabsorption of essential nutrients like vitamin B6, omega-3 fatty acids, and magnesium. Dementia and Epilepsy: Subclinical celiac disease in older adults may progress to dementia, potentially due to folic acid malabsorption. Epilepsy has also been observed in celiac patients, with brain calcifications implicated in some cases. Visual and Auditory Disturbances: Calcium channel blockages in the brain may cause visual problems, hallucinations, and migraines. These disturbances may be followed by convulsions and gastrointestinal symptoms. White Matter Lesions: MRI studies have detected T2-hyperintensive white matter lesions in some young GSE patients with neurological symptoms. Psychological Disorders Depression: Depression in GSE may result from malabsorption of vitamins and essential fatty acids or from reduced quality of life due to dietary restrictions. Depression often persists despite a GF diet, and elevated anger has also been noted. Chronic Fatigue: Chronic fatigue in GSE is systemic but has neurological components linked to blood deficiencies like anemia and vitamin/mineral deficiencies. Fatigue improves on a GF diet, though depression may worsen. Connective Tissue Disorders Arthritis: Some cases of arthritis resolve on a GF diet. Increased levels of anti-connective tissue and anti-rheumatoid factor antibodies have been found in celiac patients. Cross-reactive anti-beef-collagen antibodies may explain some rheumatoid arthritis cases. Still's Disease: An idiopathic case of Still's disease has been reported in a celiac patient. Myositis Some myopathies may result from malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins like vitamin E. GSE is also associated with immune complex glomerulonephritis and IgA nephropathy. Cancers Refractory Celiac Disease (RCD): A precancerous condition where gluten-free diets fail to resolve malabsorption. RCD is divided into two types: RCD1: Involves precancerous tissues with transformed T-cells that remain active despite gluten absence. RCD2: Involves neoplastic tissues with altered T-cell marker expression. Lymphoma: GSE increases the risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL) and other intestinal cancers. Esophageal Cancer: Squamous carcinoma of the esophagus is more prevalent in celiac disease, potentially due to GERD or vitamin A and zinc malabsorption. Adenocarcinoma: Associated with celiac disease, particularly in the bowel.
